analysis.one_liner: Lets people aged 50 to 64 buy into Medicare and rolls back last year's Medicaid cuts and paperwork rules.
analysis.headline: A single House Democrat introduced the bill on March 12, 2026; it was sent to two committees and has sat there since, with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let uninsured adults aged 50 to 64 buy into Medicare, paying premiums set to cover the program's own costs, with the same subsidies low- and middle-income people get on the ACA marketplaces. It would repeal the health provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including the Medicaid work and community-engagement requirements, and lift the income cap on ACA premium subsidies. It would also create a Medicare option that pays beneficiaries' deductibles and copays, direct Medicare to negotiate Part D drug prices, and set up a reinsurance fund to stabilize the individual insurance market.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults aged 50 to 64 who today fall into the gap before Medicare eligibility — often people who lose a job or retire early and face the highest ACA premiums of any age group. Low-income Medicaid expansion enrollees would no longer have to meet work or community-service rules to keep coverage. People with incomes above 400% of the poverty line would newly qualify for premium tax credits. Current Medicare beneficiaries could buy a public supplement covering their out-of-pocket costs, and patients would pay less for Part D drugs once Medicare negotiates prices.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare buy-in for people aged 50 to 64 who would qualify for Medicare at 65, with full Part A, B, and D benefits and the same protections, plus financial assistance similar to ACA premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions.
Repeals the health provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including the requirement that Medicaid expansion enrollees perform work, community service, or other activities to keep coverage.
Removes the 400% of poverty income cap on ACA premium tax credits and flattens the premium contribution scale, so higher-income buyers get help too.
Establishes a Medicare direct supplemental option covering deductibles, copayments, and cost-sharing for beneficiaries, community-rated with no pre-existing-condition limits.
Replaces the Part D 'noninterference' clause with a requirement that the Secretary negotiate covered drug prices with manufacturers for plan years beginning 2029.

Creates an individual market reinsurance fund paying insurers 80% of claims between $50,000 and $450,000 per high-cost enrollee, to hold down premiums, and reauthorizes ACA risk corridors for 2028 through 2031.
Appropriates $500 million per year for 2026 through 2028 for state and nonprofit outreach and enrollment, with priority to areas at risk of having no marketplace plans.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare Part D prices would be set by negotiation instead of list prices. Federal taxpayers, who fund the expanded premium tax credits, the $500-million-a-year outreach grants, and any reinsurance support beyond fees the plans themselves pay. Buy-in enrollees pay premiums sized to cover the full average cost of their care, adjusted for age and region, so the option is only as affordable as that premium and the income-based assistance layered on top.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the buy-in premium to be set so Medicare spending is not increased by the section, meaning 50-to-64-year-olds bear the full per capita cost of their own coverage; since this age group runs higher medical costs than younger marketplace buyers, premiums could be high even with the ACA-style assistance.

An optional buy-in open only to an older age band risks adverse selection — disproportionately attracting people with health problems — which pushes premiums up further; the bill responds by letting the Secretary set age-based premiums and geographic adjustments but does not guarantee affordability.
Repealing the Medicaid work requirements and expanding premium tax credits with no income cap adds substantial federal spending that the bill does not offset with new revenue.

The reinsurance fund and restored risk corridors shift the cost of the most expensive patients onto the pooled fund and other plans, a subsidy to insurers that supporters justify as premium stabilization but that also underwrites insurer margins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — a 50-to-64 Medicare buy-in, repeal of Medicaid work requirements, and uncapped premium subsidies — are large, concrete gains for people the current system prices out, at a cost mainly to drug makers and the treasury. The design is cautious rather than sweeping: premiums must be self-financing, Medicaid beneficiaries are barred from buying in, and the reinsurance program is funded largely by the plans themselves. The honest objection is affordability: a self-financing premium for a 60-year-old with modest income may still be a heavy lift, and the bill's answer is income-based assistance whose generosity depends on implementation. The insurer-facing stabilization provisions are the price of market stability but are also the bill's most industry-friendly parts.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2026 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the Medicare Expansion and Lowering Costs Now Act in the House on March 12, 2026.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means.
No other member has cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list stands at zero.
The action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action beyond the initial referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet; current law — including the Medicaid work requirements and the subsidy limits the bill would repeal — remains in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current law stands

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the two House committees with jurisdiction over health care and taxes.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and it sits in committees controlled by the House's 223 Republicans, so it has so far been a one-party effort with no Republican backing.

industries.note: The bill channels new subsidized customers and stabilization dollars through private plans: buy-in enrollees can pick Medicare Advantage plans, the reinsurance fund pays insurers 80% of high-cost claims, and risk corridors are restored for 2028-2031, while Medigap insurers get a guaranteed-issue obligation for buy-in enrollees. Insurers also face new enrollment outreach that by law excludes insurers themselves as enrollment agents.

Medicare would have to negotiate Part D drug prices with manufacturers starting in 2029, replacing the current noninterference clause. Lower negotiated prices flow to beneficiaries as lower drug costs.

Licensed independent agents and brokers working with states or nonprofits count as eligible enrollment agents for the $500-million-a-year outreach grants, though they cannot take payments from insurers for this work.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and referral to two committees run by the House's Republican majority, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in this Congress; most one-sponsor health bills at this stage die quietly when the session ends in January 2027.
